title: This week in India's growth story: November 2-8, 2026
excerpt: A week of 28 stories: a record-breaking IPO season, two separate port records broken twice over, a GDP print that beat the central bank's own forecast, and the people turning amla, aquaculture, weaving and tribal healthcare into livelihoods - alongside the scientists and civic leaders carrying India's name further than it's ever reached before.
bodyHtml:
Twenty-eight stories this week, and the pattern that kept surfacing was records breaking their own predecessors within weeks - a port breaking last month's record, an economy outrunning the forecast meant to describe it, a factory sector that eased on paper while its export orders quietly got stronger. Here's the week, day by day.

Monday, November 2

Indian companies raised a record $12.5 billion through IPOs between January and September, even as the broader stock market fell. On this day, Shreeram Abhyankar's death anniversary was marked. Srini Gopalan, who went to school in Delhi, was named CEO of T-Mobile, one of America's biggest phone companies. And Kamlesh Kumari led a Pratapgarh self-help group that turned the local amla into a business large enough for the Prime Minister to name on national radio.

Tuesday, November 3

India's crude steel output hit a new high for September - with demand growing even faster than supply could keep up. On this day in 1933, Amartya Sen was born, an economist who measured a country's progress by what its people could actually do, not just its GDP. Supinder Wraich, who came to Canada from India at age four, was named one of the country's Top 25 immigrants for 2026. And Sujata Bhuyan, an Odisha homemaker, noticed fish farming happening on a local reservoir and decided to learn the trade herself.

Wednesday, November 4

India's economy grew 7.8% in the first quarter of FY27, beating the Reserve Bank's own 7% forecast. On this day, Shakuntala Devi's birth anniversary was marked - the woman who once multiplied two 13-digit numbers in 28 seconds with no calculator and no paper. Harshan Ramadass, born in India, was elected mayor of Fernie, a Canadian mountain town, in October 2026. And Dr. Budhri Tati was recognized with a Padma Shri for nearly 40 years of walking into roughly 550 villages in a Naxal-affected Chhattisgarh district most organizations avoided.

Thursday, November 5

India's GST collections posted their fastest growth of the fiscal year, up 25.6% over the same month last year. On this day in 1817, the Battle of Khadki was fought near Pune, deciding the fate of an empire that had ruled for over a century. Sabih Khan, born in Moradabad, runs Apple's entire global operations as its COO. And Kaushalya Devi, a Gorakhpur dairy entrepreneur, started with three cows and limited market access - and a year later had earned Rs 11.5 lakh.

Friday, November 6

Jawaharlal Nehru Port set a new container throughput record for September, breaking its own record from just one month earlier. On this day in 1913, Gandhi led a march of over 2,000 miners and laborers across the Volksrust border in South Africa, and was arrested for it - twice. Sandhya "Sandy" Reddy, who grew up in a Telangana village, became mayor of Strathfield, an Australian city, in September 2026. And Purnima, recognized under the Lakhpati Didi scheme in Balrampur, Chhattisgarh, was confined to her home until a few years ago - now 400 farmers come to her for advice.

Saturday, November 7

Chennai's Container Terminal set its highest container record in a decade - and broke its own record from the month before. On this day in 1930, C.V. Raman became the first Asian ever to win a Nobel Prize in science, for noticing why the sea looks blue. Dr. Kavita Radhakrishnan, born in Mumbai and trained as an engineer, became dean of a top US nursing school. And Shobha Devi, a Bihar agri-entrepreneur, built a network that now reaches 400 farmers.

Sunday, November 8

India's factories kept expanding for yet another month, and export orders hit a six-month high even as the headline PMI eased slightly. On this day in 1917, Dr. Kamal Ranadive was born - she built India's first tissue culture research lab, then after retiring trained rural women as health workers. Prof. Zora Singh, born in a Punjab village, became the first Australian ever to win horticulture's top global honor. And Najitra Didi, who has trained women in weaving since 1984, saw her handwoven sarees cross Rs 3 lakh in sales within days.

Twenty-eight stories, one week. A record IPO season, two ports that kept breaking their own month-old records, and a GDP print that outran its own forecast - alongside the quiet four-decade careers in weaving, healthcare outreach and dairy farming that finally got their moment.
